title: Linux & Unix Systems
summary: The server your code runs on is a Unix box. Reading it — processes, signals, files, sockets — is the difference between guessing and finding the bug in 90 seconds.

blocks.markdown:
Unix is a kernel plus a swarm of small **processes** talking to it through a handful of **system calls**.

- **Unix philosophy** — many tiny programs, each doing one thing well, glued by pipes over plain text.
- **Everything is a file** — regular files, directories, devices, sockets, even kernel state in `/proc`. Same read/write calls work on all.
- **The shell** is not magic; it is just one more process that launches others and wires up their streams.
- Internalize "every process talks to the kernel, everything it touches looks like a file" and Linux becomes one consistent machine.

blocks.subTitle: The debugging toolkit
blocks.markdown:
When a box misbehaves, each tool answers one question.

| Question | Reach for |
|---|---|
| What's eating CPU/RAM now? | `top` / `htop` |
| Why is this process stuck? | `strace -p <pid>` |
| Who holds this port/file? | `ss -tlnp`, `lsof` |
| Is DNS resolving right? | `dig name` |

Most tools are just front-ends reading `/proc`.

blocks.subTitle: Streams and redirection
blocks.markdown:
Every process is born with three streams, named by small integers called **file descriptors**.

- **fd 0 = stdin** (input), **fd 1 = stdout** (output), **fd 2 = stderr** (errors). All point at your terminal by default.
- The shell quietly **re-points** them before launching: `cmd > out.txt` sends stdout to a file, `2> err.txt` sends only errors.
- `cmd > all.txt 2>&1` — stdout goes to the file, then `2>&1` makes stderr follow wherever fd 1 *currently* points. Order matters.
- stdout and stderr are **separate** — `> out.txt` alone leaves errors on your terminal.

blocks.subTitle: Pipes compose tools
blocks.markdown:
A pipe connects one program's stdout to the next program's stdin — tiny tools snap together for jobs none was written for.

```bash
grep ' 500 ' access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

- The shell makes an in-kernel **pipe** (~64 KB buffer), then launches both sides **at once** — they stream concurrently, not one-then-the-other.
- If the buffer fills, the writer **blocks** until the reader catches up — automatic back-pressure.
- That's why `tail -f log | grep error` works: it never waits for `tail` to finish.

blocks.subTitle: Processes and signals
blocks.markdown:
A **process** has a PID, its own memory, and a parent — so processes form a tree rooted at PID 1 (`init`/`systemd`).

- New processes come from **fork** (duplicate) then **exec** (replace the code).
- A **signal** is a tiny message the kernel delivers. `kill` only *sends* one; most signals don't terminate.
- **SIGTERM (15)** — "please shut down," catchable for graceful cleanup. **SIGKILL (9)** — "die now," uncatchable, no cleanup.
- **SIGHUP** conventionally means "reload config"; **SIGSTOP/SIGCONT** pause and resume.
- A **zombie** (`Z`) has exited but its parent hasn't reaped it via `wait()`.

blocks.subTitle: File permissions
blocks.markdown:
Each file has an owner, a group, and three `rwx` sets — for owner, group, and everyone else.

- Bit values: **r=4, w=2, x=1**. Sum per set: `rwxr-xr--` = `7 5 4` = `754`.
- Set with `chmod 754 file` (numeric) or `chmod g+w file` (symbolic).
- On a **directory**, `x` means "may enter/traverse" (needed to `cd` in), and `w` means "may create/delete files inside."
- Special bits: **setuid** (run as the file's owner, e.g. `passwd`) and the **sticky bit** on `/tmp` (only owners delete their own files).

blocks.subTitle: /proc and containers
blocks.markdown:
`/proc` is a **virtual filesystem** — the files don't exist on disk; the kernel generates them on read.

- `cat /proc/<pid>/status` (state, memory, parent), `ls /proc/<pid>/fd` (open descriptors), `cat /proc/loadavg`.
- `ps`, `top`, and `lsof` are just pretty front-ends reading `/proc` — so you're never blocked on a locked-down box.
- **Containers** reuse the "just Linux processes" model: **namespaces** limit what a process can *see* (PIDs, network, mounts); **cgroups** limit what it can *use* (CPU, memory, I/O).
- See [e06-containerization-deep](e06-containerization-deep.md).

blocks.subTitle: Graceful vs forceful stop
blocks.markdown:
Stopping a process is a choice between clean and certain.

- **SIGTERM** — lets the process drain requests and close files, but may hang if it's wedged.
- **SIGKILL** — guarantees death, but risks corrupt state and leaked resources.
- **Rule:** send SIGTERM, wait a grace period (~30s), then SIGKILL only if still alive.
- This is exactly what `systemd`, Docker, and Kubernetes (`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`) do.

blocks.subTitle: Pipe a one-liner or write a script
blocks.markdown:
Composed tools are fast to write; scripts are safe to repeat.

- **One-off investigation** → pipe `grep | awk | sort`. Instant, readable, throwaway.
- **Production or repeated logic** → a real script with error handling. Pipelines have none and break on weird input.
- **`strace`/`tcpdump`** reveal ground truth but slow the target or flood you — reach for logs, `ss`, `top` first, then drop down and scope tightly (`-p <pid>`, `port 443`).

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The Unix process+signal model runs the software you depend on.

- **nginx** — a master holds the listening socket and forks workers; `SIGHUP` reloads config with zero downtime, `SIGQUIT` drains gracefully.
- **systemd** — PID 1 supervises services, restarts crashes, and shuts down via SIGTERM, then a wait, then SIGKILL.
- **Redis** — snapshots by `fork()`; the child writes to disk while the parent serves, relying on copy-on-write ([b05-caching](b05-caching.md)).
- **Docker** — `docker stop` sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after a grace period.

blocks.subTitle: Narrowing a slow box
blocks.markdown:
Debugging is a method: each step narrows the search, cheap signals before expensive ones.

- **`uptime`** — load 31 on 8 cores means ~4x more work than CPUs; a resource problem, not yet logic.
- **`top`** — find the suspect PID burning CPU or growing memory.
- **`strace -p <pid>`** — 95% in `read()` on a socket means it's waiting on the network, not computing.
- **`ss -tnp`** — piles of `CLOSE_WAIT` / `SYN-SENT` reveal a connection leak to a dead dependency.
- **`dig` + `tcpdump`** — confirm whether packets even arrive.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and on-call:

- **"`kill` kills."** It only sends a signal; the default is SIGTERM. Reaching for `kill -9` too fast skips graceful shutdown.
- **"`chmod 777` fixes permissions."** It removes all protection — the real fix is usually wrong **owner/group** (`chown`).
- **"A pipe runs left fully, then right."** Both run concurrently, streaming through a live buffer.
- **"High load = high CPU."** Load also counts processes blocked in disk I/O — load 30 with idle CPUs means an I/O bottleneck.
- **"No space" with `df` free.** Out of **inodes** (`df -i`) or a **deleted-but-open file** (`lsof | grep deleted`).
